position: attributive only — almost always in *rose-colored glasses*
contrast: American spelling is *rose-colored*; British writing has *rose-coloured* or *rose-tinted*.

senses.gloss: Seeing things as better than they really are.
examples: He looks back at the nineties through *rose-colored* glasses.
Take off the *rose-colored* glasses and look at the numbers.
The report gives a *rose-colored* picture of the economy.

senses.gloss: Pink, the color of a rose.
examples: She picked a *rose-colored* fabric for the curtains.
The invitations came on *rose-colored* card stock.

contrast: *Rosy* drops the *e* of *rose*, and the *y* becomes *i* in comparison: *rosier*, *rosiest*.

senses.gloss: Pink and healthy-looking, usually about skin.
examples: The baby had *rosy* cheeks after the walk.
Her face was *rosy* from the cold.
His cheeks looked *rosier* after a week at the beach.

senses.gloss: Hopeful; promising a good future.
examples: The company painted a *rosy* picture of next year.
Things are not as *rosy* as the press release suggests.

senses.gloss: Having pink, healthy-looking cheeks.
examples: A *rosy-cheeked* boy opened the door.
The choir was full of *rosy-cheeked* kids in scarves.
She played a *rosy-cheeked* farm girl in the movie.

contrast: In New England *a rotary* is also a noun — a traffic circle. Elsewhere in the US people say *traffic circle* or *roundabout*.

senses.gloss: Turning around a center point; working by turning.
examples: The old phone had a *rotary* dial.
A *rotary* engine has no pistons going up and down.
The bakery bakes everything in a *rotary* oven.

contrast: *Rotten* fits food, wood and teeth. Milk that has gone bad is *spoiled* or *sour*, not *rotten*.

senses.gloss: Decayed and no longer good.
examples: The apples at the bottom of the bag were *rotten*.
The whole porch is *rotten* underneath.
Something smells *rotten* in the fridge.

senses.gloss: Very bad or unpleasant.
examples: We had *rotten* luck with the weather.
That was a *rotten* thing to say.
I feel *rotten* about canceling on you.

contrast: The *gh* is pronounced /f/: *rough* rhymes with *stuff*. The adverb *roughly* also means 'approximately': *roughly ten miles*.

senses.gloss: Not smooth or even to the touch.
examples: The wall was *rough* to the touch.
My hands get *rough* in the winter.
This road is *rougher* than the one we took.

senses.gloss: Difficult or unpleasant to live through.
examples: She's had a *rough* year.
It was a *rough* flight.

senses.gloss: Approximate; not finished or exact.
examples: Give me a *rough* estimate.
This is just a *rough* draft.

senses.gloss: Using force; not gentle or safe.
examples: Don't be too *rough* with the puppy.
The neighborhood used to be pretty *rough*.

senses.gloss: Rough and disorderly, but usually without real harm.
examples: *Rough-and-tumble* play is normal for puppies.
He grew up in a *rough-and-tumble* neighborhood.
She loves the *rough-and-tumble* world of city politics.

form: compound — preposition phrase used as one word
contrast: Before a noun it is the adjective *round-the-clock care*; after a verb use the adverb *around the clock*: *They worked around the clock*.

senses.gloss: Going on all day and all night without stopping.
examples: The patient needs *round-the-clock* care.
There was *round-the-clock* coverage of the trial.
The plant runs on a *round-the-clock* schedule.

contrast: In Britain *a roundabout* is a noun — a traffic circle. As an adjective meaning 'indirect' it is normal American English.

senses.gloss: Not direct — going the long way, or said in an indirect way.
examples: We took a *roundabout* route to avoid the highway.
He told me in a *roundabout* way that I hadn't gotten the job.
That's a *roundabout* explanation for something very simple.

senses.gloss: Curved, with no sharp corners or edges.
examples: The table has *rounded* corners.
Her handwriting is soft and *rounded*.
Sand the edges until they're *rounded*.

senses.gloss: Complete and balanced, covering every side of something.
examples: The school aims to give kids a *rounded* education.
She wanted a *more rounded* view of the problem.

senses.gloss: Making people excited and enthusiastic.
examples: The coach gave a *rousing* speech at halftime.
The band ended with a *rousing* version of the anthem.
The bill passed to *rousing* applause.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *a routine checkup*
contrast: The stress is on the second syllable: *roo-TEEN*. *A routine* is also a noun — a fixed order of doing things, or a dance or comedy act.

senses.gloss: Done regularly as normal procedure; ordinary.
examples: It was a *routine* traffic stop.
She's in for *routine* surgery on Thursday.
There is nothing *routine* about this case.

contrast: *A roving eye* is a set phrase for someone who keeps looking at other people romantically.

senses.gloss: Moving from place to place instead of staying in one.
examples: She works as a *roving* reporter for the network.
A *roving* band of musicians played between the tables.
The museum sends a *roving* exhibit to small towns.

senses.gloss: Noisy and rough, in a way that can cause trouble.
examples: A *rowdy* group of fans filled the bar.
The crowd got *rowdier* after the third quarter.
It was a *rowdy* wedding, in the best way.

contrast: *Royal* means 'of a king or queen'; *regal* means 'looking like royalty'. A *royal pain* has nothing to do with kings — it just means a very big nuisance.

senses.gloss: Belonging to or connected with a king or queen.
examples: The *royal* family spent the summer in Scotland.
The palace is still a *royal* residence.
She received a *royal* pardon.

senses.gloss: Complete, total — used before a few words to make them stronger.
examples: Parking downtown is a *royal* pain.
He made a *royal* mess of the kitchen.

contrast: A *rubber* mat is made of rubber; *rubbery* chicken only feels like it.

senses.gloss: Tough and bendy like rubber, usually said about badly cooked food.
examples: The calamari was *rubbery*.
Microwaved eggs come out *rubbery*.
He cut into a *rubbery* piece of steak.

senses.gloss: Red and healthy-looking, said about skin.
examples: He had a *ruddy* face from working outdoors.
Her complexion was *ruddy* after the hike.
His cheeks looked *ruddier* than usual.

senses.gloss: Very basic — only the first and simplest level.
examples: He has a *rudimentary* knowledge of Spanish.
The clinic has only *rudimentary* equipment.
Our plan is still pretty *rudimentary*.

contrast: *Unruffled* is the common opposite of the second sense: *She stayed unruffled through the whole meeting*.

senses.gloss: Pushed out of place so it is no longer smooth.
examples: The bird sat there with *ruffled* feathers.
His hair was *ruffled* from the wind.

senses.gloss: Slightly upset or annoyed.
examples: She looked a little *ruffled* by the question.
Nothing gets him *ruffled*.

senses.gloss: Made with ruffles — strips of gathered cloth.
examples: She wore a white *ruffled* blouse.
The dress has a *ruffled* hem.

contrast: The *-ed* is always /ɪd/ and makes a second syllable: *RUH-gid*, never *ruhgd*.

senses.gloss: Rough, rocky and hard to travel across.
examples: The *rugged* coastline is hard to reach by car.
We hiked through *rugged* terrain for six hours.

senses.gloss: Strong and built to survive hard use.
examples: These boots are *rugged* enough for winter work.
The laptop comes in a *rugged* case.

senses.gloss: Of a man's face: strong-featured in an attractive way.
examples: He has a *rugged*, weather-beaten face.
The ad was looking for a *rugged* type.

senses.gloss: Destroyed, with only broken remains left.
examples: We walked around a *ruined* castle above the river.
The *ruined* church is still standing after the fire.

senses.gloss: Spoiled so badly that it is no good any more.
examples: My shoes were *ruined* by the road salt.
The whole evening was *ruined* by one phone call.

senses.gloss: Causing very serious damage, especially to money or a business.
examples: The lawsuit was *ruinous* for the family business.
They borrowed at *ruinous* interest rates.
A second bad harvest would be *ruinous*.

contrast: *A ruling* is also a noun — a judge's or an official's decision.

senses.gloss: Having power over a country or an organization.
examples: The *ruling* party lost its majority.
Members of the *ruling* class sent their children abroad.
The *ruling* coalition fell apart in March.

senses.gloss: Wrinkled and messy, usually said about clothes or bedding.
examples: He showed up in a *rumpled* suit.
The sheets were *rumpled* where the cat had slept.
Her jacket looked *rumpled* after the flight.

contrast: *A rundown*, written as one word with the stress on *run*, is a noun meaning a quick summary: *Give me the rundown*.

senses.gloss: In bad condition because nobody has taken care of it.
examples: They bought a *run-down* house on the edge of town.
The whole block looks *run-down*.

senses.gloss: Tired and slightly unwell.
examples: I've been feeling *run-down* since the trip.
You look *run-down* — take a day off.

senses.gloss: Ordinary, with nothing special about it.
examples: It's a *run-of-the-mill* office job.
The food was *run-of-the-mill* diner food.
This is no *run-of-the-mill* thunderstorm.

contrast: A grammar term: a *run-on sentence* pushes two sentences together with no period and no conjunction.

senses.gloss: Of a sentence: made of two sentences joined without the right punctuation.
examples: Her essay was full of *run-on* sentences.
Fix the *run-on* sentence in the second paragraph.
A comma splice is one kind of *run-on* error.

contrast: *A runaway* is also a noun — a child or teenager who has left home.

senses.gloss: Having escaped or left home without permission.
examples: The shelter takes in *runaway* teens.
A *runaway* horse blocked the road for an hour.

senses.gloss: Out of control and impossible to stop.
examples: A *runaway* truck hit the barrier on the hill.
*Runaway* inflation wiped out their savings.

senses.gloss: Won very easily; extremely successful.
examples: The movie was a *runaway* hit.
She won the primary in a *runaway* victory.

contrast: In *running shoes* and *running track*, *running* is a noun used as a modifier, not an adjective. *Three days running* is an adverb meaning 'in a row'.

senses.gloss: Of water: flowing, especially from a tap.
examples: The cabin has no *running* water.
Rinse the rice under *running* water.

senses.gloss: Continuing over a long time, with new parts added.
examples: It's a *running* joke in our family.
Keep a *running* total as you shop.
They have a *running* argument about the thermostat.

senses.gloss: More liquid than it should be.
examples: The sauce came out *runny*.
I like my eggs a little *runny*.
This batter is *runnier* than the recipe says.

senses.gloss: Of a nose or eyes: producing liquid because of a cold or an allergy.
examples: She has a *runny* nose and a cough.
My eyes get *runny* every spring.

contrast: *Rural* is a neutral fact of geography; *rustic* adds old-fashioned charm. A city restaurant can look *rustic*, never *rural*.

senses.gloss: In or about the countryside, away from cities.
examples: She grew up in *rural* Kansas.
*Rural* hospitals are closing all over the state.
The area north of the lake is still very *rural*.

senses.gloss: Done too fast, without enough time to do it well.
examples: The ending of the movie felt *rushed*.
We ate a *rushed* breakfast and ran for the train.

senses.gloss: Of a person: forced to hurry.
examples: I felt *rushed* the whole morning.
Don't let them make you feel *rushed*.

contrast: Russian *православный* on its own is *Orthodox* or *Eastern Orthodox*; *Russian Orthodox* names the Russian church in particular. Both words take a capital letter.

senses.gloss: Belonging to the Orthodox church of Russia.
examples: They were married in a *Russian Orthodox* church in Brooklyn.
His grandmother is *Russian Orthodox*.
*Russian Orthodox* Christmas falls on January 7.

contrast: *Russian-speaking* is about the language, not the country: a *Russian-speaking* family may be from Kazakhstan or Israel. After a verb say *They speak Russian*.

senses.gloss: Using Russian as an everyday language.
examples: The clinic is looking for a *Russian-speaking* nurse.
There is a large *Russian-speaking* community in Brighton Beach.
She joined a *Russian-speaking* book club.

contrast: *Rustic* is a compliment about style — plain and country-like. *Rural* is only about location.

senses.gloss: Plain and old-fashioned in a country way that people find charming.
examples: The restaurant has a *rustic* look — bare wood and iron lamps.
We rented a *rustic* cabin with a wood stove.
The bread is dense and *rustic*.

senses.gloss: Covered with rust.
examples: A *rusty* nail was sticking out of the board.
The gate gets *rustier* every year.

senses.gloss: Of a skill: weaker than it was because you have not practiced.
examples: My Spanish is pretty *rusty*.
He's *rusty* after two years off the ice.

form: -less — literally 'without ruth', an old word for pity

senses.gloss: Willing to hurt people to get what you want; showing no pity.
examples: He was *ruthless* with anyone who slowed the project down.
It's a *ruthless* business.
She made a *ruthless* cut to the budget.

contrast: *A Rwandan* is also the noun for a person from Rwanda.

senses.gloss: From or relating to Rwanda.
examples: The *Rwandan* team qualified for the tournament.
He teaches *Rwandan* history at the community college.
Her husband is *Rwandan*.

contrast: American spelling is *saber*; British writing has *sabre-toothed*.

senses.gloss: Having very long, curved upper teeth — said of certain extinct cats.
examples: The museum has a *saber-toothed* cat skeleton.
Kids always want to see the *saber-toothed* tiger.
*Saber-toothed* predators died out about ten thousand years ago.

contrast: The adjective ends in *-e*: *saccharine*. *Saccharin*, with no *e*, is the noun for the artificial sweetener.

senses.gloss: So sweet and sentimental that it feels fake.
examples: The movie ends on a *saccharine* note.
He sang it in a *saccharine* voice.
The card's message was a little *saccharine* for my taste.

takes: *to* + person or group (*sacred to the Lakota*)
contrast: The *-ed* is /ɪd/ and makes a second syllable: *SAY-krid*. *Sacred* covers religion and deep respect; *holy* is stronger and almost always religious.

senses.gloss: Connected with religion and treated with religious respect.
examples: The mountain is *sacred* to several tribes.
The choir sang *sacred* music at the service.

senses.gloss: Too important to change, break or joke about.
examples: Sunday dinner is *sacred* in this family.
Nothing was *sacred* in his comedy.

contrast: *A sacrificial lamb* is a set phrase for the person blamed or given up so that others are protected.

senses.gloss: Offered up or given up, especially so that something else is saved.
examples: The manager became the *sacrificial* lamb after a bad season.
Ancient texts describe a *sacrificial* altar on the hill.
He made a *sacrificial* move to protect his queen.

contrast: Watch the spelling: *sacrilegious* has *-rileg-*, not *-relig-*, even though it is about religion.

senses.gloss: Treating something holy — or something people deeply respect — with disrespect.
examples: Wearing shoes inside the temple would be *sacrilegious*.
Putting ketchup on it is practically *sacrilegious* in Chicago.
The church called the painting *sacrilegious*.

senses.gloss: So important that nobody is allowed to change or question it.
examples: In this office, Friday afternoons are *sacrosanct*.
The contract is not *sacrosanct* — we can renegotiate.
He treats his grandmother's recipe as *sacrosanct*.

senses.gloss: Enjoying other people's pain or fear.
examples: The coach had a *sadistic* sense of humor.
It felt *sadistic* to make them run in that heat.
He plays a *sadistic* villain in the new series.

position: predicative only — after *be*, *arrive*, *get home* and similar verbs
contrast: A fixed phrase, always in this order and only after a verb: *They got home safe and sound*, never *a safe and sound child*.

senses.gloss: Not hurt and no longer in danger, after something risky.
examples: The hikers were found *safe and sound* the next morning.
Call me when you get there *safe and sound*.
All three kids came back *safe and sound*.

contrast: *Sage* is also a noun — the herb, and a word for a wise old person. As an adjective it sounds slightly literary; everyday English says *wise*.

senses.gloss: Wise, in a calm and experienced way.
examples: She gave me some *sage* advice about buying a house.
The column is full of *sage* observations.
A *sage* nod was all the answer I got.

senses.gloss: Hanging down in the middle under its own weight.
examples: We had to replace the *sagging* porch roof.
The old mattress was *sagging* in the middle.

senses.gloss: Falling or getting weaker, about sales, prices or spirits.
examples: *Sagging* sales forced the store to close.
They tried to lift the team's *sagging* morale.

contrast: *Sub-Saharan Africa* means the part of the continent south of the desert, and is far more common in the news than *Saharan* alone.

senses.gloss: Of or from the Sahara desert.
examples: A cloud of *Saharan* dust reached Florida last summer.
The plant survives in *Saharan* conditions.
*Saharan* nights can be surprisingly cold.

contrast: *Saintly* ends in *-ly* but is an adjective, not an adverb: *saintly patience*, never *He smiled saintly*.

senses.gloss: Extremely good, patient and forgiving.
examples: She had *saintly* patience with the twins.
Nobody is *saintly* at six in the morning.
He was *saintly* about the whole mess.

contrast: *Salacious* is about sexual detail served up for gossip. It is stronger and far more disapproving than *racy*.

senses.gloss: Full of sexual detail, in a way meant to shock or excite.
examples: The tabloid ran the *salacious* details on page one.
The book was banned as *salacious* in 1928.
He kept the story alive with *salacious* rumors.

contrast: A *salaried* worker is paid a fixed amount per year; an *hourly* worker is paid by the hour. In the US the difference decides who gets overtime.

senses.gloss: Paid a fixed yearly salary rather than by the hour.
examples: *Salaried* employees don't punch a clock.
She moved from an hourly job to a *salaried* position.
The company has about two hundred *salaried* staff.

contrast: Nothing to do with salt. It means 'standing out as important', and is most often met in *the salient points*.

senses.gloss: Standing out as the most noticeable or important.
examples: Let me go over the *salient* points of the contract.
The *most salient* fact is that nobody was home.
Her age is not *salient* here — her experience is.

contrast: *Saline* is a technical word from medicine and chemistry. Food that tastes of salt is *salty*, never *saline*.

senses.gloss: Containing salt; made of a salt solution.
examples: The nurse flushed the line with *saline* solution.
Wash the wound with a *saline* rinse.
The lake is highly *saline*.

contrast: *Salted* means salt was added — *salted butter*. *Salty* describes the taste: *The soup is too salty*.

senses.gloss: With salt added, for taste or to keep it from spoiling.
examples: Use *salted* butter for the topping.
A bowl of *salted* peanuts came with the drinks.
*Salted* caramel is on every dessert menu now.

takes: *about* + noun or *-ing* — in the slang sense
contrast: The slang sense is everywhere in American speech: *Why are you so salty?* means 'Why are you so annoyed?'

senses.gloss: Tasting of salt, or containing a lot of it.
examples: The soup is too *salty*.
Ocean air feels *salty* on your skin.
This batch is *saltier* than the last one.

senses.gloss: Annoyed or bitter about something, in American slang.
examples: He's still *salty* about not getting picked.
Don't get *salty* with me — I warned you.

contrast: *Salvadoran* is the usual American form; *Salvadorian* also appears. The country's name keeps the article: *El Salvador*.

senses.gloss: From or relating to El Salvador.
examples: There's a great *Salvadoran* bakery on the corner.
She's *Salvadoran* on her mother's side.
*Salvadoran* pupusas are worth the drive.

senses.gloss: Still able to be saved, repaired or rescued.
examples: Only the engine was *salvageable* after the fire.
Is the friendship still *salvageable*?
They sorted the wet books into *salvageable* and ruined piles.

position: both — always with *the*, *this* or *that*: *the same street*, *They look the same*
takes: *as* + noun or clause (*the same as mine*)
contrast: Always *the same*, never *a same*. Compare with *as*, not *like* and never *than*: *the same as mine*. Russian *такой же* and *одинаковый* are both *the same*: *Our phones are the same*.

senses.gloss: Not another one; exactly this one and no other.
examples: We've lived on the *same* street for twenty years.
She asked me the *same* question twice.
Your jacket is the *same* as mine.

senses.gloss: Not changed from before.
examples: The town looks the *same* as it did in 1990.
He's still the *same* old Dave.

contrast: *A Samoan* is also the noun for a person, and *Samoan* is the name of the language.

senses.gloss: From or relating to Samoa or American Samoa.
examples: The team's best lineman is *Samoan*.
We went to a *Samoan* church service on the island.
She teaches *Samoan* dance on Saturdays.

contrast: *Sanctimonious* is always an insult — it means acting morally better than everyone else. The neutral words are *devout* and *religious*.

senses.gloss: Acting as if you are morally better than other people.
examples: Spare me the *sanctimonious* lecture about recycling.
He gets *sanctimonious* whenever the topic comes up.
The editorial struck a *sanctimonious* tone.

senses.gloss: Covered with sand, or made mostly of sand.
examples: We found a long *sandy* beach south of town.
The soil here is *sandy* and dries out fast.
The path got *sandier* closer to the dunes.

senses.gloss: Of hair: light yellowish brown.
examples: He has *sandy* hair and freckles.
Her eyebrows are *sandy*, almost blond.

contrast: The noun is *sanity*. In everyday speech *insane* often just means 'crazy' or even 'amazing': *That concert was insane*.

senses.gloss: Mentally healthy; not mentally ill.
examples: The court found him *sane* enough to stand trial.
Long walks are what keeps me *sane*.

senses.gloss: Sensible and reasonable.
examples: Let's set a *sane* deadline for once.
A *saner* approach would be to test it first.

contrast: A formal word. Everyday English says *optimistic* or *hopeful*.

senses.gloss: Cheerfully confident that things will turn out well.
examples: She's *sanguine* about the company's chances.
Analysts are less *sanguine* than they were in March.
He took a *sanguine* view of the delay.

contrast: Russian *санитарный* matches only the technical sense. English also uses *sanitary* to mean 'clean enough to be safe': *That counter isn't sanitary*.

senses.gloss: Having to do with keeping places clean and free of disease.
examples: The kitchen failed a *sanitary* inspection.
*Sanitary* conditions in the camp were poor.

senses.gloss: Clean enough to be safe.
examples: Eating off that counter isn't very *sanitary*.
They keep the prep area *sanitary*.

contrast: American spelling is *-ized*; British writing has *sanitised*.

senses.gloss: Cleaned thoroughly so that germs are killed.
examples: All the equipment is *sanitized* between classes.
The tray came out *sanitized* and still warm.

senses.gloss: With the unpleasant or embarrassing parts taken out.
examples: The textbook gives a *sanitized* version of the war.
It was a *sanitized* retelling for children.

contrast: An American informal word; the British equivalent is *soppy*. It teases rather than attacks.

senses.gloss: Too sentimental, in a silly and slightly embarrassing way.
examples: We watched a *sappy* Christmas movie.
The card was *sappy*, but I kept it.
His toast got *sappier* with every glass of wine.

contrast: *Sarcastic* is saying the opposite of what you mean in order to mock someone. *Ironic* is wider and usually aimed at no one.

senses.gloss: Saying the opposite of what you mean, to mock or criticize.
examples: 'Great job,' he said, *sarcastic* as ever.
Don't be *sarcastic* with your teacher.
She made a *sarcastic* comment about my parking.

contrast: *Sardonic* is darker and quieter than *sarcastic* — a *sardonic* smile mocks without a word being said.

senses.gloss: Mocking in a dark, unamused way.
examples: He gave a *sardonic* smile and went back to his coffee.
The narrator has a *sardonic* sense of humor.
Her tone was dry and *sardonic*.

contrast: A formal, often playful word. It describes choices, style and splendor — never a person directly: *his sartorial taste*, not *a sartorial man*.

senses.gloss: Having to do with clothes and the way someone dresses.
examples: His *sartorial* choices got more attention than his speech.
The piece is about *sartorial* trends in menswear.
She arrived in full *sartorial* splendor.

contrast: An American word. About a child it is a complaint; about an adult or a style it is usually a compliment.

senses.gloss: Cheeky and rude, especially about answering back.
examples: Don't get *sassy* with your grandmother.
He was a *sassy* five-year-old.

senses.gloss: Lively, bold and confident, often about style.
examples: She showed up in a *sassy* red dress.
The ad copy is *sassier* than anything they've run before.

senses.gloss: Of the devil; evil in a religious sense.
examples: The town panicked over rumors of a *satanic* cult.
The band leaned into *satanic* imagery.
He called the whole scheme *satanic*.

contrast: *Satiric* is a rarer form of the same word. Do not confuse it with *satisfactory* or with *sarcastic*, which is about a person's tone, not a work.

senses.gloss: Using humor and exaggeration to criticize people or institutions.
examples: The magazine runs a *satirical* column every week.
It's a *satirical* novel about Wall Street.
The piece is *satirical*, not a real news report.

contrast: *Satisfactory* means 'good enough', not 'good' — a *satisfactory* grade is barely passing. *Satisfying* is about pleasure: *a satisfying meal*.

senses.gloss: Good enough for the purpose, but no better than that.
examples: The repair work was *satisfactory*.
We need a *satisfactory* explanation by Friday.
Her condition is listed as *satisfactory*.

senses.gloss: Completely soaked through.
examples: My jacket was *saturated* by the time I got home.
The ground is *saturated* after three days of rain.

senses.gloss: Holding as much as it possibly can.
examples: The market is *saturated* with delivery apps.
Butter is high in *saturated* fat.
The photo has deep, *saturated* colors.

contrast: Nothing to do with sauce on food. It is a slightly old-fashioned, playful word for 'cheeky' or 'a little risqué'.

senses.gloss: Bold and cheeky, often in a flirty way.
examples: She sent him a *saucy* postcard from Miami.
The show is famous for its *saucy* jokes.
His answer was a little *saucier* than the judge liked.

contrast: *Saudi* alone is the usual adjective; *Saudi Arabian* is also correct. *A Saudi* is the noun for a person.

senses.gloss: From or relating to Saudi Arabia.
examples: The *Saudi* delegation arrived on Tuesday.
He works for a *Saudi* airline.
Most of the students in the program are *Saudi*.

contrast: Often written with the accent: *sautéed*. It means fried quickly in a little fat, not deep-fried.

senses.gloss: Cooked quickly in a pan with a little butter or oil.
examples: The steak came with *sauteed* mushrooms.
Add the *sauteed* onions to the pot.
She served *sauteed* spinach with lemon.

contrast: Calling people *savage* in the old sense of 'primitive' is offensive today. The living uses are 'very violent' and, in slang, 'brutally blunt'.

senses.gloss: Very violent or fierce.
examples: The dog gave him a *savage* bite.
It was a *savage* storm, even for February.

senses.gloss: Extremely harsh, about criticism.
examples: The review was *savage*.
She wrote a *savage* takedown of the proposal.

senses.gloss: Brutally blunt in a way people find funny, in slang.
examples: His reply was *savage*.
That comeback was straight-up *savage*.

contrast: American spelling *savory*; British *savoury*. *Not savory* about a person or a business means shady: *a less than savory character*.

senses.gloss: Salty or spicy rather than sweet.
examples: Do you want something sweet or *savory* for breakfast?
The bakery makes *savory* hand pies.

senses.gloss: Tasting good in a rich, salty way.
examples: The broth was deep and *savory*.
Mushrooms add a *savory* note to the sauce.

contrast: American *sawed-off*; British *sawn-off*. Used of a person it is an informal, rude way of saying 'short'.

senses.gloss: Cut short with a saw, especially of a shotgun.
examples: Police recovered a *sawed-off* shotgun from the trunk.
He kept a *sawed-off* broom handle behind the counter.
The workbench stands on *sawed-off* table legs.

contrast: In American English *Anglo-Saxon* is far more common; *Saxon* on its own is mostly historical.

senses.gloss: Of the Saxons, a Germanic people who settled in England, or of Saxony in Germany.
examples: The village church has a *Saxon* tower.
He wrote his thesis on *Saxon* law.
The porcelain is *Saxon*, from the Meissen works.

contrast: Common in business and technology: something *scalable* can grow much bigger without being rebuilt.

senses.gloss: Able to grow much larger without breaking or being redesigned.
examples: The model isn't *scalable* beyond a few hundred users.
They wanted a *scalable* business, not a boutique.
We picked a *more scalable* database this time.

contrast: Spelled *scaly*, with no *e* before the *-y*.

senses.gloss: Covered with scales, or with dry, flaking skin.
examples: The lizard's *scaly* back caught the light.
My elbows get *scaly* in the winter.
His skin was *scalier* than the doctor expected.

contrast: Russian *скандальный* can mean simply 'quarrelsome'; English *scandalous* always involves shock or disgrace. A noisy neighbor is *difficult*, not *scandalous*.

senses.gloss: Shocking and morally wrong; causing public outrage.
examples: The memo revealed *scandalous* spending.
It's *scandalous* that the building is still unsafe.
She wrote a book about the family's *scandalous* past.

contrast: *Scandinavian* usually means Denmark, Norway and Sweden. *Nordic* is wider and takes in Finland and Iceland too.

senses.gloss: From or relating to Scandinavia.
examples: The store sells *Scandinavian* furniture.
Her grandparents were *Scandinavian*.
He's taking a *Scandinavian* literature class.

contrast: *Scant* goes straight before a noun, often before a number: *a scant two weeks*. After a verb use *scarce* or *not enough*.

senses.gloss: Barely any; much less than is needed.
examples: There is *scant* evidence for either theory.
The report got *scant* attention from the press.

senses.gloss: Just a little under the amount named.
examples: Add a *scant* teaspoon of salt.
We finished in a *scant* three hours.

contrast: About information *scanty* is close to *scant*, but *scant* only stands before a noun. About clothing only *scanty* works.

senses.gloss: Too small in amount.
examples: The evidence is *scanty* at best.
They lived on *scanty* rations that winter.

senses.gloss: Of clothing: covering very little of the body.
examples: She wore a *scanty* costume for the number.
The outfits got *scantier* as the show went on.

contrast: *Scarce* is about supply — there is not enough of it. *Rare* is about how seldom something occurs: *a rare bird*, but *scarce housing*. The adverb *scarcely* means 'hardly'.

senses.gloss: Not available in the amount people need; hard to get.
examples: Affordable apartments are *scarce* downtown.
Water became *scarcer* every week of the drought.
Good news has been *scarce* this year.

contrast: *Scarlet* is a bright red leaning to orange; *crimson* leans to purple. *Scarlet fever* is a children's illness.

senses.gloss: Bright, strong red.
examples: She wore a *scarlet* coat to the parade.
The maples turn *scarlet* in October.
The book's cover is plain *scarlet*.

contrast: Do not confuse *scarred* with *scared* (испуганный). They sound different too: *SKAHRD* against *SKAIRD*.

senses.gloss: Marked with scars.
examples: His hands were *scarred* from years of kitchen work.
The old table is *scarred* with knife marks.

senses.gloss: Emotionally damaged by something painful.
examples: She was *scarred* by the divorce.
A whole generation was *scarred* by the war.

contrast: *Scary* is the thing that frightens you; *scared* is how you feel. Russian *страшный* covers both: *a scary movie* leaves you *scared*.

senses.gloss: Frightening.
examples: That was the *scariest* part of the ride.
It's *scary* how fast kids grow.
We watched a *scary* movie with all the lights on.

form: -ing from *scathe*, an old verb meaning 'to harm'
contrast: Almost always about words: *a scathing review*, *scathing criticism*. People are not usually called *scathing*.

senses.gloss: Extremely harsh in its criticism.
examples: The Times ran a *scathing* review.
She sent a *scathing* email to the whole department.
His report was *more scathing* than anyone expected.

senses.gloss: Forgetful and disorganized.
examples: I've been so *scatterbrained* since the baby came.
He's a brilliant but *scatterbrained* professor.
She left the keys in the door again — totally *scatterbrained*.

senses.gloss: Spread out over an area instead of being together.
examples: Toys were *scattered* all over the floor.
Her family is *scattered* across three states.

senses.gloss: Happening here and there rather than everywhere, about weather and outages.
examples: *Scattered* showers are expected this afternoon.
There were *scattered* power outages overnight.

senses.gloss: Of a person: unable to keep track of things.
examples: I'm a little *scattered* today — I didn't sleep.
He sounded *scattered* on the phone.

form: compound — verb + noun, from the way shotgun pellets spread out
contrast: An American word, and a criticism: it says an effort had no focus, not that it was fast.

senses.gloss: Done in a broad, unfocused way, with no real plan.
examples: Their marketing is *scattershot* — a little of everything.
He took a *scattershot* approach to job hunting.
The essay is *scattershot* but full of good lines.

contrast: *The scenic route* is the longer, prettier way — Americans often say it as a joke after getting lost.

senses.gloss: Having beautiful natural views.
examples: We took the *scenic* route along the coast.
There's a *scenic* overlook two miles up the road.
The drive through the pass is the *most scenic* part of the trip.

contrast: *Scented* means a smell was added on purpose; *fragrant* means it smells good on its own. American products are labeled *unscented* or *fragrance-free*.

senses.gloss: Given a pleasant smell, usually on purpose.
examples: She lit a *scented* candle.
We bought *scented* soap for the guest bathroom.
He hates *scented* laundry detergent.

contrast: Americans say *SKEJ-ool*; the British say *SHED-yool*. A *scheduled* flight is a regular service, not a charter.

senses.gloss: Planned to happen at a particular time.
examples: The *scheduled* departure is 6:40.
*Scheduled* maintenance will close the line tonight.
The meeting ran past its *scheduled* end.

contrast: *A schematic* is also a noun — a wiring or circuit diagram. About writing, *schematic* is a criticism: too simple to feel real.

senses.gloss: Shown as a simple diagram, with only the main parts.
examples: The manual includes a *schematic* drawing of the circuit.
He gave a *schematic* outline of the plan.
The characters are *schematic* — more types than people.
